title: Bit Manipulation and Byte Ordering

sections.heading: Byte Ordering: Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian
sections.body:
A multi-byte word occupies several consecutive memory addresses; **byte ordering** (endianness) is the convention for which of its bytes sits at the lowest address. Write a $w$-byte word as bytes $b_{w-1} b_{w-2} \ldots b_1 b_0$, most significant first, so the value is

$$x = \sum_{i=0}^{w-1} b_i \cdot 256^i.$$

If `addr(x)` denotes the address of the word, **big-endian** stores $b_{w-1}$ at `addr(x)`; **little-endian** stores $b_0$ at `addr(x)`. Nothing about the value or the arithmetic on it changes between the two conventions — only which byte-sized slice of memory you touch when reading fewer than $w$ bytes at a time, or exchanging raw bytes with another machine.

x86-64 and (in its default mode) ARM64 are little-endian, so a CENG331 lab machine, and every datalab/attacklab binary built for it, stores the least significant byte first; Y86-64, the teaching ISA built for the same course, is specified to store words in little-endian order too, matching the real machine it models. This matters the moment a program reads a multi-byte value one byte at a time — through a `char *`, a `union`, or a network socket. The course's own illustration overlays a `union` of `unsigned char c[8]`, `unsigned short s[4]`, `unsigned int i[2]` and `unsigned long l[1]` on the same eight bytes and prints each view in hex: writing sequential bytes `0xf0..0xf7` into `c[]` and reading `i[0]` back gives `0xf3f2f1f0` on x86-64, not `0xf0f1f2f3`.

Two conventions collide in networking: TCP/IP headers are transmitted **big-endian** ("network byte order") regardless of the host's own convention, which is why BSD sockets code calls `htonl`/`ntohl`/`htons`/`ntohs` before putting a multi-byte field on the wire — on a little-endian host these byte-swap; on a big-endian host they are no-ops. Historically SPARC and IBM mainframes are big-endian; ARM is *bi-endian* and can run either way. The cheapest runtime test, with no library call, is to write 1 through an `int *` and read it back through a `char *`: if the low-addressed byte is 0, the machine is big-endian.

sections.heading: Shifts: Logical vs. Arithmetic
sections.body:
Left shift `x << k` always fills the vacated low bits with 0 and behaves identically whether `x` is signed or unsigned: it computes $x \cdot 2^k \bmod 2^w$, i.e. multiplication by $2^k$ with silent high-order truncation. Right shift comes in two forms that differ only in what fills the vacated *high* bits. **Logical** shift fills with 0 unconditionally; **arithmetic** shift replicates the sign bit $b_{w-1}$. C mandates logical shift for unsigned operands, but for *signed* operands the standard leaves the choice implementation-defined; in practice every mainstream compiler on a two's-complement machine (GCC, Clang, MSVC, on x86-64 or ARM64) chooses arithmetic shift.

The consequence is that `x >> k` on a negative signed `x` computes $\lfloor x / 2^k \rfloor$ — rounding toward $-\infty$ — which is *not* the value C's own `/` operator gives, since integer division rounds toward zero; the two agree only when $x$ is an exact multiple of $2^k$. The course material calls this "round away from zero" for negative numbers (further from 0 than truncation) and notes the fix: **biasing**. Adding $2^k - 1$ before shifting converts the arithmetic shift's round-toward-$-\infty$ into the round-toward-zero that `/` produces:

$$\left\lfloor \frac{x + 2^k - 1}{2^k} \right\rfloor_{\text{shift}} = \mathrm{trunc}(x / 2^k) \quad \text{for } x < 0.$$

x86-64 encodes the logical/arithmetic distinction directly: `sal` and `shl` are two mnemonics for the identical left-shift opcode; `sar` performs arithmetic right shift, `shr` logical. All four take the shift amount either as an immediate or from register `%cl`, but only the low $\log_2 w$ bits of `%cl` are used, not saturated: with `%cl = 0xFF`, `salb` (8-bit operand) shifts by 7, `salw` (16-bit) by 15, `sall` (32-bit) by 31, and `salq` (64-bit) by 63. A C-level shift by a negative amount or by an amount $\ge w$ is undefined behavior precisely because the language makes no such masking guarantee — the hardware's masked result depends on the exact instruction the compiler chose to emit.

sections.heading: Masks, Bit Idioms, and the XOR Swap
sections.body:
Given a $k$-bit field starting at bit position $p$ of word `x`, extract it with `(x >> p) & ((1 << k) - 1)`: the mask `(1 << k) - 1` has its low $k$ bits set and every other bit 0. The same mask sets the field with `x | mask`, clears it with `x & ~mask`, and toggles it with `x ^ mask`. Two idioms built from a mask and the value itself recur across almost every bit-manipulation routine. `x & (x - 1)` **clears the lowest set bit**: subtracting 1 flips every bit from the lowest set bit down to bit 0 (turning `...1000` into `...0111`) and leaves every higher bit unchanged, so ANDing with the original removes exactly that one bit. `x & (-x)` **isolates the lowest set bit**: in two's complement, `-x` equals `~x + 1`, and adding 1 to `~x` ripples a carry exactly up to and including the position of `x`'s lowest set bit, reproducing that bit and every bit below it identically to `x` while inverting everything above it — so ANDing the two leaves only that one bit set.

The **XOR swap**, `x ^= y; y ^= x; x ^= y;`, exchanges two variables without a temporary. It works because XOR is associative, commutative, its own inverse ($a \oplus a = 0$), and has 0 as an identity element, so each line rewrites one variable as the XOR of the original pair. It is a curiosity rather than good practice for two reasons: it silently zeroes both variables if `x` and `y` alias the same storage location (`x ^= x` is always 0), and on any pipelined machine it is slower than three ordinary moves, because the three XORs form a serial dependency chain — each reads the register the previous instruction just wrote — that the hardware cannot execute out of order the way it could three independent `mov`s.

sections.heading: Counting Bits: Popcount and Trailing Zeros
sections.body:
A naive population count tests all $w$ bits of `x` one at a time, costing exactly $w$ iterations no matter the value. **Brian Kernighan's trick** instead repeats `x &= x - 1` until `x` is 0: since each iteration clears exactly one set bit — the same fact that justifies the masking idiom above — the loop runs exactly `popcount(x)` times, at most $w$ but often far fewer for sparse inputs, and no worse than the naive loop even when `x` is dense. Trailing-zero count reduces to the companion idiom: `lowbit = x & (-x)` leaves a single 1 bit standing, and its position is `ctz(x)`. Finding that position can be a shift-and-test loop, but it can also be done in $O(1)$: multiply `lowbit` by a precomputed **De Bruijn constant** and use the top few bits of the product to index a small lookup table. This works because a de Bruijn sequence of order $\log_2 w$ contains every possible $\log_2 w$-bit substring exactly once as a cyclic window, so multiplying a single isolated bit by the constant produces a distinct, recoverable pattern in the high bits for every one of the $w$ possible bit positions.

Modern x86-64 exposes both operations directly in hardware. `POPCNT` (SSE4.2) computes population count at roughly 3-cycle latency, 1-per-cycle throughput; `TZCNT`/`LZCNT` (BMI1) compute trailing/leading zero count similarly and, unlike the older `BSF`/`BSR` they replace, are architecturally defined to return $w$ — not an undefined result — at input 0. GCC and Clang expose this through `__builtin_popcount`, `__builtin_ctz` and `__builtin_clz`: with the right target flags (`-mpopcnt`, `-mbmi`) they compile straight to the hardware instruction, and otherwise fall back to Kernighan's loop or a constant-time SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) formula.

sections.heading: Data-Lab Constraints and Undefined Behavior
sections.body:
CS:APP's Data Lab restricts many puzzles to a deliberately tiny operator subset — typically just `~`, `&`, `^`, `|`, `+`, and shifts, with no conditionals, loops, or comparison operators — to force a re-derivation of boolean identities at the gate level. **De Morgan's laws**, `x & y == ~(~x | ~y)` and `x | y == ~(~x & ~y)`, let a solution trade one forbidden operator for two permitted ones. A recurring puzzle family asks for a boolean property of a value — all bits equal, the sign, whether it is exactly 0 — collapsed into a single 0/1 result without `==` or `!=`; the standard move is to combine a shift that isolates or replicates the sign bit with a mask, since `x >> (w - 1)` (arithmetic) turns a negative `x` into all-ones and a non-negative `x` into all-zeros in a single instruction.

Two undefined-behavior traps deserve separate emphasis from ordinary bugs, because they change a program's meaning silently rather than crashing it. First, shifting by a negative amount or by an amount $\ge w$ is undefined in C — the `%cl`-masking behavior above is a property of the *hardware instruction* the compiler emits, not a guarantee from the *language*, so the same source recompiled for a different target is free to do something else. Second, left-shifting a signed value so a 1 bit crosses the sign position is undefined, even though every mainstream compiler defines a concrete two's-complement answer for it. Both are exactly the "implementation detail of a real system" the course tests as fast recall rather than derivation — METU's own midterm asks for a `char *`-based `isBigEndian()` one-liner bundled with a two's-complement conversion, in the same few-point warm-up question, rather than a proof of either.

code.caption: Endianness detection, logical vs. arithmetic shift, and the popcount/ctz idioms in one runnable program.

worked_example.problem:
An `int x` holds the value $-1{,}234{,}567{,}890$ at address `0x2000` on an x86-64 machine.

(a) Give x's 32-bit two's-complement representation in hex.

(b) Lay out its four bytes at addresses `0x2000`–`0x2003`, once little-endian and once big-endian.

(c) Compute `x >> 5` (arithmetic) and `(unsigned)x >> 5` (logical) in decimal, then compare the arithmetic-shift result to C's own `x / 32`.

(d) Separately, trace Brian Kernighan's popcount and find `ctz` on the 8-bit pattern `0xB4`.
worked_example.solution:
**(a) Two's-complement hex.** $2^{32} = 4{,}294{,}967{,}296$, so

$$-1{,}234{,}567{,}890 \bmod 2^{32} = 3{,}060{,}399{,}406 = \mathtt{0xB669FD2E}.$$

**(b) Byte layout.** The four bytes, most significant first, are `B6 69 FD 2E`.

| Address | 0x2000 | 0x2001 | 0x2002 | 0x2003 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Big-endian | `B6` (MSB) | `69` | `FD` | `2E` (LSB) |
| Little-endian | `2E` (LSB) | `FD` | `69` | `B6` (MSB) |

**(c) Shifts.** In binary, $x = \mathtt{0xB669FD2E}$ has its sign bit set, so:

$$x \texttt{ >> 5 (arithmetic)} = \left\lfloor \frac{-1234567890}{32} \right\rfloor = -38{,}580{,}247.$$

$$\texttt{(unsigned)}x \texttt{ >> 5 (logical)} = 95{,}637{,}481.$$

C's `x / 32` truncates toward zero and gives $-38{,}580{,}246$ — one *more* than the arithmetic shift, confirming the shift rounds toward $-\infty$ ("away from zero" for a negative dividend) while `/` rounds toward zero; adding the bias $2^5 - 1 = 31$ before shifting, $(x + 31) \texttt{ >> } 5$, gives exactly $-38{,}580{,}246$, matching `/`.

**(d) Kernighan's trick and ctz on `0xB4`.** In binary, $\mathtt{0xB4} = \texttt{10110100}$, so bits 2, 4, 5 and 7 are set.

| Iter. | `x` before | `x - 1` | `x &= x - 1` | bit cleared |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `10110100` | `10110011` | `10110000` | bit 2 (`0x04`) |
| 2 | `10110000` | `10101111` | `10100000` | bit 4 (`0x10`) |
| 3 | `10100000` | `10011111` | `10000000` | bit 5 (`0x20`) |
| 4 | `10000000` | `01111111` | `00000000` | bit 7 (`0x80`) |

The loop runs 4 times, so `popcount(0xB4) = 4`, matching the four 1-bits counted directly. The *first* bit cleared is always the lowest one, at bit 2, so `ctz(0xB4) = 2` — consistent with `lowbit = x & (-x) = 0x04`.

pitfalls: **Assuming `>>` on `int` is always arithmetic.** It is implementation-defined in C; nearly universal in practice on two's-complement targets, but code that depends on it is not portable, and Java deliberately gives `>>` and `>>>` separate, precise meanings for this reason.

**Shifting by ≥ the operand width or by a negative amount.** Undefined behavior in C, even though x86-64 quietly masks the shift amount to `%cl`'s low bits — a different target or a different optimization level is free to produce a different answer.
**Confusing `-x` with `~x`.** Bitwise complement flips every bit; two's-complement negation is `~x + 1`. Using one where the other is meant silently shifts every result off by one.

**Applying `x & (x - 1)` or `x & (-x)` to `x == 0`.** Both compute 0, which is often the desired sentinel, but a `ctz` built from `x & (-x)` must special-case 0 explicitly since `BSF`/`__builtin_ctz` leave the result of a zero input undefined; `TZCNT` does not.

**Reaching for the XOR swap for performance.** Its three sequentially dependent instructions are slower on a pipelined machine than three independent `mov`s, and it corrupts data outright when the two operands alias the same location.

**Forgetting byte order when serializing.** Writing a `struct` straight to a file or socket bakes in the host's endianness; reading it back on a machine with the opposite convention silently reinterprets every multi-byte field.
applications: **BSD sockets / network protocols.** TCP/IP headers are big-endian on the wire; `htonl`/`ntohl` convert to and from host order, byte-swapping only on little-endian hosts such as x86-64.

**Bitboards in chess engines.** A 64-bit integer represents piece occupancy per square; move generation repeatedly isolates and clears the lowest set bit with `x & (-x)` and `x &= x - 1` to iterate over occupied squares.

**Bloom filters and hash-based sketches.** Setting/testing k bits per key is pure mask-and-shift arithmetic, and estimating the number of distinct bits set (as in HyperLogLog) leans on `ctz`/`clz` of hashed values.

**Kernel and glibc bitmap operations.** Linux's `find_first_bit`/`find_next_bit` and the buddy allocator's free-list bitmaps are built from the same clear-lowest-bit and isolate-lowest-bit idioms, compiled down to `TZCNT`/`BSF` where available.

**Compiler builtins.** GCC/Clang's `__builtin_popcount`/`__builtin_ctz`/`__builtin_clz` are the portable entry point real codebases use instead of hand-rolled loops, selecting hardware instructions when the target ISA supports them.
exam_focus: CENG331's MT-2019 midterm warm-up (Question 1) asks students to write `int isBigEndian(void)` that returns 1 on a big-endian machine and 0 on little-endian, using only a `char *` cast and no library calls — the canonical pointer-based endianness test.

The same warm-up question bundles the endianness test with a 3-point sub-question asking for the 16-bit two's-complement hex representation of a small negative number, signalling that CENG331 treats these bit-level representation facts as fast, few-point recall rather than derivation.

CENG331 lecture slides present logical vs. arithmetic right shift as a worked bit-diagram table (an 8-bit argument, then `<< 3`, `logical >> 2`, `arithmetic >> 2` for two sample values) — expect shift questions in this exact tabular, trace-the-bits format.

The XOR swap is introduced explicitly as a named challenge ("can you swap without a temporary variable?") with a three-step bit-level trace, which is the form a short-answer question on it would take.

self_check.question: Why does the C standard leave the behavior of `>>` on signed integers implementation-defined, while `>>` on unsigned integers is always precisely logical shift?
self_check.answer: An unsigned value has no reserved sign bit, so there is only one sensible way to fill vacated high bits: with 0. A signed value's top bit doubles as its sign, and the 'correct' fill for that bit depends on the machine's representation: on a two's-complement machine, replicating the sign bit (arithmetic shift) preserves the algebraic sign and gives a useful `floor(x / 2^k)` semantics, but C's standard predates universal two's-complement hardware and historically had to accommodate sign-magnitude and ones'-complement machines, where no single shift rule is 'correct' for all of them. The standard therefore left the choice to the implementation instead of mandating one. In practice, every mainstream compiler on a two's-complement target (which is effectively all of them today) chooses arithmetic shift for signed `>>`, so the ambiguity is a portability footnote rather than a live hazard — except for code that is compiled with unusual flags or ported to unusual hardware.

self_check.question: METU's MT-2019 midterm asks for the 16-bit `short int` representation of $-42$ in hexadecimal. Derive it, showing the two's-complement construction.
self_check.answer: A 16-bit two's-complement representation of a negative value $x$ is $x \bmod 2^{16}$. Equivalently, take the 16-bit binary representation of $42$, complement every bit, and add 1. $42 = \texttt{0000 0000 0010 1010}$. Complementing gives $\texttt{1111 1111 1101 0101}$; adding 1 gives $\texttt{1111 1111 1101 0110} = \mathtt{0xFFD6}$. Check by reduction: $2^{16} - 42 = 65536 - 42 = 65494 = \mathtt{0xFFD6}$, which agrees. So the 16-bit short representation of $-42$ is $\mathtt{0xFFD6}$.

self_check.question: Using only bitwise operators (no loops, no `%`, no `/`), how would you (i) test whether a 64-bit unsigned integer is an exact power of two, and (ii) round it up to the next power of two? Explain why each expression is correct.

key_points: Big-endian stores the MSB at the lowest address; little-endian (x86-64, ARM64, Y86-64) stores the LSB there instead.
Left/unsigned-right shift are always logical; signed right shift is implementation-defined but arithmetic in practice.
Arithmetic right shift computes floor(x / 2^k), not C's round-to-zero division, for negative x not divisible by 2^k.
x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit; x & (-x) isolates it — both underlie popcount, ctz and power-of-two tests.
POPCNT and TZCNT/LZCNT give O(1) hardware bit counts; software falls back to Kernighan's loop or a De Bruijn lookup.
Shifting by a negative amount or by ≥ the operand width is undefined behavior in C, whatever the hardware actually does.
tagline: Endianness fixes which byte sits lowest in memory; masks, shifts and popcount/ctz tricks manipulate the bits inside each byte.
tldr: Byte ordering (endianness) decides which byte of a multi-byte word sits at the lowest address — **little-endian** on x86-64, ARM64 and Y86-64, **big-endian** on the network wire. Left shift is always logical; right shift is **logical** for unsigned values and, in every mainstream compiler, **arithmetic** for signed ones, so `x >> k` computes $\lfloor x/2^k \rfloor$ rather than C's round-to-zero division. The idioms `x & (x-1)` and `x & (-x)` clear and isolate the lowest set bit respectively, and underlie both Brian Kernighan's popcount loop and $O(1)$ trailing-zero counts via a De Bruijn lookup or the hardware `POPCNT`/`TZCNT` instructions.
